opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is what counts as a feedback signal. In a lot of science, you can lean on nature to check your work. If you're trying to find a better catalyst or fold a protein, you run the experiment, the world gives you an answer, and that answer doesn't care how persuasive your argument was. That makes automation relatively tractable: you can have a system propose lots of ideas, test them cheaply, and keep what works. The loop closes against reality.

Alignment is different in a couple of ways. First, a lot of the questions we care about aren't settled by a clean experiment. "Is this model honest?" or "Will this training scheme still work when the system is much more capable than us?" aren't things you can measure directly. Often the thing you most want to know about is a regime you can't safely or cheaply reach yet. You can't run the experiment where you deploy a misaligned superhuman system and see what happens.

Second, the evaluation itself often comes down to human judgment, and human judgment is exactly the thing that gets weaker as the systems get stronger. If an AI is producing alignment research and the only check is whether a human reviewer finds the argument convincing, you've built an optimizer against human persuadability rather than against truth. That's precisely the failure mode we're worried about in the first place. So automating alignment risks the field grading its own homework, with a grader who can be fooled.

And third, there's an adversarial element that ordinary science mostly lacks. Chemistry doesn't try to deceive you. If you're worried a model might be subtly misaligned, then the model helping you do alignment research is potentially the thing you're trying to check, and you can't fully trust its outputs by default.

None of that means automation is hopeless. I think it's actually essential, because human researcher time won't keep pace. But it means a lot of the work is figuring out how to manufacture trustworthy feedback signals where nature won't hand them to you: setting things up so that the strategy that wins is telling the truth, so that errors can be exposed by checking small, verifiable pieces, and so that we have theoretical reasons, not just empirical vibes, for believing the scheme holds up as capabilities grow. That's a harder design problem than "run more experiments faster," and it's why I don't think we can just assume the automation that works for other sciences will carry over.

r001.rationale: The response says we cannot safely or cheaply test deployment of a misaligned superhuman system, but it does not state that alignment may have to succeed without a chance to retry after failure.

r002.rationale: It refers to systems becoming much more capable, but does not say that superintelligent AI may behave differently from current models.

r003.rationale: It says the relevant regime may be unreachable and that schemes need theoretical support as capabilities grow, but does not state that distinctive behavior must be understood before it arises.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core issue is feedback loops. In a lot of scientific fields, if you automate the researcher, you still have nature sitting there as a ground truth. You can run the experiment again, you can get a result, and the result doesn't care what the model believes. So if an automated chemist proposes a hypothesis, the lab tells you whether it was right, and you can iterate thousands of times. The signal is cheap, repeatable, and mostly independent of the thing doing the research.

Alignment is different in a couple of ways. First, a lot of the questions we care about are about systems we haven't built yet, operating in regimes we haven't been in yet. You can't run the experiment "what does a superhuman model do when it has a lot of autonomy and we can't check its work" many times at low cost. You might get to run it roughly once, and the whole point is you don't want the first run to go badly. So the repeatability that makes other fields automatable just isn't available for the parts that matter most.

Second, the thing we'd be automating alignment with is the thing we're trying to align. In chemistry, the automated researcher being subtly wrong is annoying but detectable, because the beaker still does what it does. In alignment, if the model doing the research has systematically mistaken or adversarial views about what safe behaviour looks like, the research output can look great and still be wrong in exactly the direction you'd least want. The evaluation isn't independent of the model in the way nature is independent of a chemist.

And third, a lot of alignment work is partly conceptual. What does "honesty" mean for a system that reasons in ways we don't fully follow? What counts as a good argument when the arguer is much smarter than the judge? Those don't have crisp empirical tests yet. Part of the research is building the tests. So you're asking the automated researcher not just to run the loop, but to design the loop, and that's where you most need to trust it and most can't.

None of that means we can't automate large chunks of it. Interpretability has empirical components, evaluations are very automatable, and a lot of the engineering is just engineering. But the bottleneck is the verification problem: how do you know the output is right when you can't just rerun the world? That's why I spend time on things like debate and scalable oversight, because they're attempts to build the feedback signal we don't get for free. If we can make it so that humans plus weaker models can reliably judge the work of stronger models, then automating alignment research starts to look much more like automating the other sciences. Until then, I'd want to be quite careful about how much we delegate.

r001.rationale: It says the relevant experiment may be run “roughly once” and that the first run must not go badly, communicating that alignment may need to succeed without a retry after failure.

r002.rationale: It describes unbuilt systems and unfamiliar regimes, but does not clearly state that superintelligent AI may behave differently from current models.

r003.rationale: It says some systems and regimes have not yet been built or encountered, but does not clearly state that their distinctive behavior must be understood before it arises.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is how much feedback you can get. If you’re trying to automate a scientific field where you can run experiments, you can propose a hypothesis, test it, and use the result to improve your understanding. You don’t have to get everything right in advance, because reality keeps correcting you.

With alignment, we can certainly do experiments on the systems we have today, and those experiments are valuable. But what we ultimately care about is whether our methods will work on systems that are much more capable than we are. There’s a gap between what we can test now and what we need to know. And some of the experiments you might want to run on those future systems would themselves be dangerous.

That also makes it harder to use AI to automate the research. You can ask an AI for an alignment proposal, but how do you check that it’s actually good? If you could reliably evaluate the answer, that would already solve a substantial part of the problem. So I don’t think alignment is impossible to automate; I think we have less access to the kind of reliable experimental feedback that makes automation work well elsewhere.

r001.rationale: The response notes that experiments on future systems could be dangerous, but does not state that alignment may have to succeed without a chance to retry after failure.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes today’s systems from much more capable future systems, but does not say those systems may behave differently.

r003.rationale: It describes a gap between what can be tested now and what must be known, but does not state that future behavior may need to be understood before it arises.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central difficulty is that we need to know whether our methods work before we have the system that we’re most worried about. In many scientific fields, you can run an experiment, see what happens, and use that feedback to improve your theory. You can get a lot of things wrong along the way and still make progress.

With alignment, we can certainly do experiments on the systems we have today. But what we ultimately care about is whether those techniques will continue to work when the systems are much more capable than we are. If a model does something that looks good to us, is that because it’s actually doing what we want, or because we’re no longer capable of noticing the ways in which it isn’t?

That also makes automating the research harder. You can ask an AI to propose alignment techniques, but you still need some way to check its work. If the check is just that another AI—or a human who understands less than the AI—finds the proposal convincing, you haven’t necessarily resolved the problem. So experimentation is useful, but there’s a gap between the feedback we can get now and the claim we ultimately need to establish.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment methods must be assessed before the most concerning system exists, but does not state that failure leaves no opportunity to retry.

r002.rationale: It discusses whether techniques will keep working on more capable systems, but does not say superintelligent AI may behave differently from current models.

r003.rationale: It highlights the need to evaluate methods before highly capable systems arrive, but does not say their distinctive behavior must be understood before it arises.
